e: The mesencephalon (midbrain) surrounds the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius, not a '2nd ventricle.' There is no standard 2nd ventricle; the brain ventricles are the paired lateral ventricles, third, and fourth.
k: Mesencephalon surrounds the cerebral aqueduct, not a 2nd ventricle

e: The cerebral hemispheres contain deep grey matter nuclei such as the basal ganglia and thalamus. In the spinal cord, grey matter is central and H-shaped. The brainstem has grey matter surrounded by white matter, and the cerebellar cortex is grey matter externally.
k: Cerebral hemispheres contain deep grey matter nuclei; spinal cord grey matter is central, white matter peripheral

e: A ganglion is a collection of cell bodies outside the CNS. A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers within the CNS. A nucleus is a collection of cell bodies within the CNS. A lemniscus is a collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem. A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibers outside the CNS.
k: Ganglion = peripheral cell bodies; nucleus = central cell bodies; tract/lemniscus = CNS fiber bundles

e: A nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies within the CNS. A ganglion is the equivalent in the PNS. Nerve fibers form tracts or nerves, not nuclei.
k: Nucleus = cluster of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS

e: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers within the CNS. A pathway is a chain of successive tracts with the same function. A lemniscus is a collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem. Afferent means input toward a structure. A ganglion is a group of cell bodies outside the CNS.
k: Tract = CNS fiber bundle; pathway = chain of tracts; lemniscus = ascending brainstem fibers

e: A pathway is a chain of successive tracts in the CNS serving the same function. A fasciculus is a smaller bundle within a tract. A lemniscus is a specific ascending brainstem pathway. A commissure connects two sides of the CNS, and a decussation is a midline crossing.
k: Pathway = chain of successive tracts with identical function

e: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers in the CNS sharing the same origin, termination, and function. A pathway is a chain of tracts. A lemniscus is an ascending brainstem bundle. A commissure connects hemispheres, and a decussation is a crossing.
k: Tract = CNS fiber bundle with common origin, termination, and function

e: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3), a branch of the cervical plexus, supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland. The infraorbital and mental nerves supply the upper and lower lips.
k: Great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies skin over the angle of the mandible

e: The lobule is the soft, fleshy lower part of the auricle (earlobe). The tragus is the small pointed projection anterior to the ear canal. The concha is the bowl-shaped depression.
k: Lobule = soft lower part of the auricle (earlobe)

e: The cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) descends into the neck to supply the platysma muscle. The temporal, zygomatic, and buccal branches supply facial muscles above the mouth.
k: Cervical branch of facial nerve innervates the platysma

e: The internal carotid artery enters the skull through the carotid canal and supplies the forehead via the supraorbital and supratrochlear branches of the ophthalmic artery. It does not supply the chin, cheek, or temple.
k: Internal carotid artery supplies the forehead via ophthalmic branches

e: The infraorbital nerve, a terminal branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2), exits through the infraorbital foramen to supply skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose.
k: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the upper lip

e: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland. The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the temple and anterior auricle.
k: Great auricular nerve supplies skin over the angle of the mandible

e: The infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose. The supraorbital nerve (V1) supplies the upper eyelid and forehead.
k: Infraorbital nerve (V2) carries sensation from the lower eyelid

e: The central part of the upper lip drains primarily to the submandibular lymph nodes. The upper lip also drains to the submental nodes via lymphatic crossing. The buccal and parotid nodes drain more lateral facial regions.
k: Central upper lip drains to submandibular lymph nodes

e: The ala of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2) laterally and the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (V1) at the tip.
k: Ala of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve (V2) and external nasal nerve (V1)

e: The zygomaticotemporal branch of the zygomatic nerve (V2) supplies the non-hairy skin of the temple region. The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the scalp of the temple.
k: Zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the non-hairy temple region

e: The internal carotid artery supplies the forehead via branches of the ophthalmic artery. Injury to the forehead region would lead to blood loss from the internal carotid system. The chin and cheek are supplied by external carotid branches.
k: Forehead injury can lead to internal carotid blood loss

e: The infraorbital nerve (V2) exits through the infraorbital foramen and supplies the skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip, and lateral side of the nose. Loss of sensation indicates injury to this nerve.
k: Infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the lower eyelid skin

e: The greater occipital nerve is the medial branch of the dorsal ramus of C2. It supplies the skin of the occipital region of the scalp. The auriculotemporal, great auricular, lesser occipital, and posterior auricular nerves are ventral ramus derivatives.
k: Greater occipital nerve = dorsal ramus of C2

e: The transverse facial artery, a branch of the superficial temporal artery (external carotid), runs above the parotid duct. The facial artery enters the face at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter.
k: Transverse facial artery lies above the parotid duct

e: The tip of the nose is supplied by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (ophthalmic division, V1). Therefore, numbness suggests damage to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
k: Tip of the nose sensation = ophthalmic division (V1) via external nasal branch

e: The occipital group of lymph nodes lies at the apex of the posterior triangle and drains the posterior scalp region behind the ear.
k: Scalp behind the ear drains to occipital lymph nodes

e: The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, supplies the scalp in the temporal region and the skin over the anterior auricle.
k: Auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the scalp via the temporal region

e: The lateral part of the upper eyelid drains to the parotid (pre-auricular) lymph nodes. The medial part drains to the submandibular nodes.
k: Lateral upper eyelid drains to parotid lymph nodes

e: The skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3), which arises from the cervical plexus.
k: Angle of mandible = C2–C3 via great auricular nerve

e: The cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) descends to supply the platysma muscle in the neck.
k: Cervical branch of facial nerve (CN VII) → platysma

e: The buccinator muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), specifically via its buccal branches. Although it is in the region of the mandibular nerve, the motor supply is from the facial nerve.
k: Buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII)

e: Subperiosteal hematoma is localized and takes the shape of the underlying bone because the periosteum is firmly attached to the skull sutures, limiting spread.
k: Subperiosteal hematoma takes the shape of the underlying bone due to periosteal attachment at sutures

e: The two frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle originate from the skin of the eyebrows and interdigitate with the orbicularis oculi. They are not attached to the superior temporal line.
k: Frontal bellies of occipitofrontalis originate from skin of eyebrows

e: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland, and the scalp behind the auricle.
k: Great auricular nerve (C2–C3) supplies scalp behind the auricle

e: The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of the maxillary and superficial temporal veins. It begins inside the parotid gland, is deep to the facial nerve, and divides into anterior and posterior branches.
k: Retromandibular vein = maxillary + superficial temporal; lies deep to facial nerve in parotid

e: The lacrimal part of the orbicularis oculi is attached to the lacrimal sac and the posterior lacrimal crest. It helps drain tears by compression of the lacrimal sac.
k: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi attaches to lacrimal sac and aids tear drainage

e: The orbicularis oris muscle originates from the modiolus (a fibromuscular condensation at the angle of the mouth) and inserts into the lips. It acts as the sphincter of the mouth.
k: Orbicularis oris originates from the modiolus

e: The mandibular nerve (V3) carries sensation from the lower lip (via the mental nerve), chin, temporal region, and anterior ear. It does not supply the upper eyelid, lower eyelid, or tip of the nose.
k: Mandibular nerve (V3) sensory supply includes the lower lip and chin

e: The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery. It has a tortuous course to accommodate jaw movements and ends at the medial angle of the eye.
k: Facial artery has a tortuous course and anastomoses with ophthalmic branches at the medial eye angle

e: The facial artery can be palpated as it crosses the lower border of the mandible at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter muscle.
k: Facial artery pulse is palpable at the anteroinferior angle of the masseter

e: Bell's palsy is facial nerve (CN VII) palsy. It causes inability to close the eyelids and facial muscle weakness. Hearing is generally unaffected; in fact, sounds may seem louder (hyperacusis) due to stapedial nerve involvement.
k: Bell's palsy does NOT cause weaker hearing; hyperacusis may occur due to stapedial nerve involvement

e: The parotid capsule is innervated by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3), which carries pain fibers from the gland capsule.
k: Parotid capsule pain is carried by the great auricular nerve (C2–C3)

e: Bleeding into the loose areolar connective tissue layer of the scalp allows blood to spread freely and gravitate into the eyelids via the subaponeurotic space, causing a black eye.
k: Loose areolar tissue layer bleeding causes black eye via gravitational spread

e: The scalp has numerous sebaceous glands associated with hair follicles. Its rich vascularity means wounds bleed profusely, and aponeurotic wounds gape due to muscle pull.
k: Scalp has abundant sebaceous glands; wounds bleed profusely and gape if aponeurosis is cut

e: Infection spreads most readily in the loose areolar connective tissue layer because it contains valveless emissary veins that can transmit infection intracranially.
k: Loose areolar tissue is the dangerous layer of the scalp due to valveless emissary veins

e: The scalp moves as a single unit because the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and epicranial aponeurosis are firmly attached. The plane of movement is between the epicranial aponeurosis and the pericranium.
k: Scalp movement occurs between epicranial aponeurosis and pericranium

e: The large blood vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense subcutaneous connective tissue layer, which is richly vascularized and innervated.
k: Blood vessels and nerves of the scalp run in the dense subcutaneous connective tissue layer

e: The great auricular nerve (C2–C3) derives from the cervical plexus, not the trigeminal nerve. All other listed nerves are branches of the trigeminal nerve.
k: Great auricular nerve (C2–C3) is NOT a branch of the trigeminal nerve

e: The occipitofrontalis muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), specifically the temporal and posterior auricular branches. The great auricular and great occipital nerves are purely sensory.
k: Occipitofrontalis muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII)

e: The infraorbital nerve (branch of maxillary division, V2) is the main sensory nerve of the upper lip, lower eyelid, and cheek.
k: Infraorbital nerve (V2) is the main sensory nerve of the upper lip

e: The mental nerve, a terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular division, V3), exits through the mental foramen to supply the skin of the lower lip and chin.
k: Mental nerve (V3) is the main sensory nerve of the lower lip

e: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi has bony attachments both medially (medial palpebral ligament) and laterally (lateral palpebral raphe). Therefore, the statement that it has no medial bony attachment is incorrect.
k: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi has bony attachments medially and laterally

e: Lateral upper eyelid → lacrimal nerve (V1). Tip of nose → external nasal nerve (V1). Lower lip → mental nerve (V3). Angle of mandible → great auricular nerve (C2–C3). Forehead → supraorbital nerve (V1).
k: Specific facial skin areas have distinct sensory nerve supplies

e: The superficial temporal artery, a terminal branch of the external carotid artery, can be palpated in front of the tragus of the ear against the zygomatic arch.
k: Superficial temporal artery pulse is palpable anterior to the tragus against the zygomatic arch

e: The occipitofrontalis muscle elevates the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead. The frontalis portion inserts into the epicranial aponeurosis.
k: Occipitofrontalis elevates the eyebrows

e: Facial muscles are sphincters and dilators of facial openings. They are supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the hypoglossal nerve.
k: Facial muscles act as sphincters for facial orifices and are innervated by CN VII

e: The orbital part of the orbicularis oculi is responsible for firm (forced) closure of the eyelids. The palpebral part closes the eye gently.
k: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi = forced eye closure; palpebral part = gentle closure

e: The orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eyelids. The levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) opens the eyelid.
k: Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids

e: The buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII) via its buccal branches. It is NOT innervated by the mandibular nerve.
k: Buccinator is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the mandibular nerve

e: The orbicularis oris is the sphincter muscle of the lips. The buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth during chewing.
k: Orbicularis oris = sphincter of the lips

e: Skin = common site for sebaceous cysts. Epicranial aponeurosis = attached to superior temporal line. Loose connective tissue = dangerous layer. Pericranium = continuous with sutural ligaments. Dense connective tissue = wounds do not gape.
k: Loose areolar tissue is the dangerous layer of the scalp due to emissary veins

e: The subcutaneous connective tissue layer of the scalp is dense and fibrous. Infections here are localized because the tissue is dense. Wounds bleed profusely because fibrous septa prevent vasoconstriction.
k: Subcutaneous connective tissue of scalp is dense; infection is localized and wounds bleed profusely

e: The two occipital bellies of the occipitofrontalis are separated by the median tendinous intersection and take origin from the lateral two-thirds of the highest nuchal line.
k: Occipital bellies originate from the highest nuchal line

e: The venous drainage of the face is primarily via the facial vein into the internal jugular vein. Tributaries include the supraorbital, supratrochlear, external nasal, and labial veins. The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein and with the pterygoid plexus via the deep facial vein. Infections in the 'danger triangle' can spread to the cavernous sinus.
k: Facial vein drains into internal jugular and communicates with cavernous sinus
m: The venous drainage of the face is primarily via the facial vein, which drains into the internal jugular vein. Important tributaries include the supraorbital, supratrochlear, external nasal, and superior and inferior labial veins. The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein and the pterygoid plexus via the deep facial vein. Clinically, infections in the 'danger triangle of the face' (upper lip, nose, medial eye) can spread to the cavernous sinus, causing thrombosis.

e: The facial artery branches in the neck include ascending palatine, tonsillar, and glandular branches. In the face, it gives inferior labial, superior labial, and lateral nasal branches, ending as the angular artery. It anastomoses with the infraorbital branch of the maxillary artery, the transverse facial artery, and branches of the ophthalmic artery.
k: Facial artery anastomoses with ophthalmic, maxillary, and transverse facial branches
m: The facial artery gives off branches in the neck (ascending palatine, tonsillar, glandular) and in the face (inferior labial, superior labial, lateral nasal). It terminates as the angular artery at the medial angle of the eye. It anastomoses with the infraorbital branch of the maxillary artery, the transverse facial artery, and branches of the ophthalmic artery (supratrochlear, supraorbital).

e: The arteries of the scalp include: (1) Supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries (from ophthalmic, internal carotid). (2) Superficial temporal artery (from external carotid). (3) Posterior auricular artery (from external carotid). (4) Occipital artery (from external carotid).
k: Scalp arteries: supraorbital/trochlear (internal carotid), superficial temporal, posterior auricular, occipital (external carotid)
m: The arteries of the scalp are: (1) Supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries (branches of the ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid). (2) Superficial temporal artery (terminal branch of the external carotid). (3) Posterior auricular artery (branch of the external carotid). (4) Occipital artery (branch of the external carotid). The supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries arise from the ophthalmic artery.

e: Nerves of the scalp in front of the auricle include: (1) Auriculotemporal nerve (V3). (2) Temporal branch of facial nerve (CN VII, motor). (3) Great auricular nerve (C2–C3). (4) Lesser occipital nerve (C2).
k: Scalp nerves anterior to auricle: auriculotemporal (V3), temporal branch of facial nerve, great auricular (C2–3), lesser occipital (C2)
m: Nerves of the scalp in front of the auricle include: (1) Auriculotemporal nerve (branch of mandibular division V3), supplying the temporal region and anterior auricle. (2) Temporal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), motor to the frontalis. (3) Great auricular nerve (C2–C3), supplying the angle of the mandible and lower parotid region. (4) Lesser occipital nerve (C2), supplying the upper lateral neck.

e: Nerves of the scalp behind the auricle include: (1) Greater occipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C2). (2) Lesser occipital nerve (C2, ventral ramus). (3) Greater auricular nerve (C2–C3). (4) Posterior auricular nerve (CN VII, motor).
k: Scalp nerves posterior to auricle: greater occipital (C2 dorsal), lesser occipital (C2 ventral), great auricular (C2–3), posterior auricular (CN VII)
m: Nerves of the scalp behind the auricle include: (1) Greater occipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C2), supplying the occipital scalp. (2) Lesser occipital nerve (ventral ramus of C2), supplying the upper lateral neck and lower lateral scalp. (3) Great auricular nerve (C2–C3), supplying the angle of the mandible. (4) Posterior auricular nerve (branch of CN VII), motor to the occipitalis and auricular muscles.

e: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches into the lacrimal, frontal, and nasociliary nerves. The frontal nerve divides into the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves, supplying the forehead and scalp. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral upper eyelid. The nasociliary nerve gives the infratrochlear nerve and anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves.
k: Ophthalmic nerve (V1) branches: lacrimal, frontal (supraorbital/supratrochlear), nasociliary
m: The ophthalmic nerve (V1) gives rise to the lacrimal, frontal, and nasociliary nerves. The frontal nerve divides into the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves, supplying the forehead and scalp. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral part of the upper eyelid. The nasociliary nerve gives the infratrochlear nerve, anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves, and the long ciliary nerves.

e: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives the zygomatic nerve (zygomaticotemporal and zygomaticofacial branches), the infraorbital nerve, and branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion. It exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.
k: Maxillary nerve (V2) branches: zygomatic, infraorbital, pterygopalatine ganglion branches
m: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives the zygomatic nerve (which divides into zygomaticotemporal and zygomaticofacial branches), the infraorbital nerve (supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper lip), and branches to the pterygopalatine ganglion. It exits the skull via the foramen rotundum.

e: The mandibular nerve (V3) has sensory branches including the buccal nerve (cheek), auriculotemporal nerve (temple), lingual nerve (tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (mental nerve for lower lip and chin). It exits via the foramen ovale.
k: Mandibular nerve (V3) branches: buccal, auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar (mental)
m: The mandibular nerve (V3) has sensory branches including the buccal nerve (cheek skin and mucosa), auriculotemporal nerve (temple and anterior auricle), lingual nerve (anterior two-thirds of tongue), and inferior alveolar nerve (which gives the mental nerve for the lower lip and chin). It exits the skull via the foramen ovale.

e: The facial nerve gives the posterior auricular nerve in the neck before entering the parotid gland. Its five terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. The cervical branch supplies the platysma.
k: Facial nerve terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical
m: The facial nerve gives off the posterior auricular nerve in the neck before entering the parotid gland. Within and beyond the parotid, it divides into five terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. The cervical branch supplies the platysma.

e: The orbicularis oculi has three parts: (1) Orbital part: outer thick portion, forceful eye closure. (2) Palpebral part: thin portion in eyelids, gentle closure/blinking. (3) Lacrimal part: deep portion attached to lacrimal sac, aids tear drainage.
k: Orbicularis oculi parts: orbital (forced closure), palpebral (gentle closure), lacrimal (tear drainage)
m: The orbicularis oculi has three parts: (1) Orbital part: the outer thick portion attached to the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments; responsible for forceful eye closure. (2) Palpebral part: the thin portion in the eyelids; responsible for gentle closure (blinking). (3) Lacrimal part: the deep portion attached to the lacrimal sac; aids tear drainage via the lacrimal canaliculi.

e: The facial vein lacks valves and communicates with the cavernous sinus via the ophthalmic veins. Squeezing an abscess in the upper lip (danger triangle) can force infected thrombi into the cavernous sinus, causing thrombosis.
k: Upper lip abscess → risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis via valveless facial vein

s.text: What is the name of sinus at risk?
s.explanation: The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via valveless ophthalmic veins, making it the sinus at risk.
s.keyConcept: Facial vein → cavernous sinus via ophthalmic veins

s.text: Describe 2 alternate pathways for passage of infection to the sinus.
s.modelAnswer: First pathway: via the superior ophthalmic vein connecting the angular vein to the cavernous sinus. Second pathway: via the deep facial vein connecting the facial vein to the pterygoid plexus, which connects to the cavernous sinus via emissary veins.
s.explanation: The facial vein has two main connections to the cavernous sinus: directly via the superior ophthalmic vein and indirectly via the deep facial vein to the pterygoid plexus.
s.keyConcept: Facial vein connects to cavernous sinus via superior ophthalmic vein and pterygoid plexus

s.text: What other areas have similar risk?
s.modelAnswer: The medial angle of the eye, the nose, and the cheeks share similar venous drainage to the facial vein and thus carry the same risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis if infected.
s.explanation: These areas drain into the facial vein and its tributaries, which communicate with the cavernous sinus without valves.
s.keyConcept: Danger triangle includes medial eye, nose, and upper lip

e: The scalp has a rich blood supply and dense connective tissue that prevents vessel constriction, leading to profuse bleeding. The dangerous layer is the loose areolar tissue because it contains valveless emissary veins.
k: Scalp wounds bleed profusely due to rich vascularity and inability to constrict

s.text: Why does the scalp bleed profusely?
s.modelAnswer: Because the scalp has a rich blood supply and the fibrous tissue in the connective tissue layer prevents the local vasoconstriction of the blood vessels in this layer.
s.explanation: The dense fibrous septa in the scalp's subcutaneous layer tether the vessels open, preventing vasoconstriction and causing profuse bleeding.
s.keyConcept: Scalp dense fibrous tissue prevents vasoconstriction → profuse bleeding

s.text: Name the arteries that supply the scalp.
s.modelAnswer: Arteries supplying the scalp in front of the auricle: supraorbital artery, supratrochlear artery, and superficial temporal artery. Behind the auricle: posterior auricular artery and occipital artery.
s.explanation: The scalp is supplied by five paired arteries: supraorbital and supratrochlear (internal carotid), and superficial temporal, posterior auricular, and occipital (external carotid).
s.keyConcept: Five arteries supply the scalp: supraorbital, supratrochlear, superficial temporal, posterior auricular, occipital

s.text: Which is the dangerous layer of the scalp? Why is it dangerous?
s.modelAnswer: Loose areolar tissue layer because it contains the emissary veins that are valveless and can take infection to the inside of the skull.
s.explanation: The loose areolar tissue contains valveless emissary veins that communicate with intracranial venous sinuses, allowing infection to spread intracranially.
s.keyConcept: Loose areolar tissue contains valveless emissary veins → intracranial spread

e: Scalp bleeding requires suturing because dense connective tissue prevents vasoconstriction. Gaping indicates aponeurosis involvement. Black eye results from blood tracking through loose areolar tissue to the eyelids. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a dangerous complication.
k: Scalp wound complications: profuse bleeding, black eye, cavernous sinus thrombosis

s.text: Why scalp bleeding cannot be stopped except by suturing?
s.modelAnswer: Because the scalp has a rich blood supply and the fibrous tissue in the connective tissue layer prevents the local vasoconstriction of the blood vessels in this layer.
s.explanation: Dense fibrous septa in the subcutaneous tissue hold vessels open, preventing natural vasoconstriction.
s.keyConcept: Scalp dense fibrous tissue prevents vasoconstriction → requires suturing

s.text: Gaping of scalp wound indicates involvement of which layer of scalp?
s.modelAnswer: Gaping of scalp wound indicates involvement of aponeurosis of occipito-frontalis muscle.
s.explanation: The epicranial aponeurosis is inelastic; when cut, the frontalis and occipitalis muscles retract, causing the wound to gape.
s.keyConcept: Aponeurosis cut → wound gapes due to muscle retraction

s.text: Explain the development of black eye.
s.modelAnswer: If the wound causes subaponeurotic hematoma, the blood gravitates to the eyelids deep to the frontal bellies of the occipito-frontalis muscle which are attached to the skin of eyebrows, and so hematoma extends deep to it and reaches eyelids causing black eye.
s.explanation: Blood in the subaponeurotic layer tracks anteriorly beneath the frontalis to the eyelids due to gravity.
s.keyConcept: Subaponeurotic hematoma tracks to eyelids → black eye

s.text: What dangerous complication did the doctor expect?
s.explanation: Infected blood from the scalp can spread via emissary veins to the cavernous sinus, causing thrombosis.
s.keyConcept: Scalp infection can spread via emissary veins → cavernous sinus thrombosis

e: The spinal dura mater extends from the foramen magnum to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2), where it fuses with the filum terminale to form the coccygeal ligament.
k: Spinal dura mater ends at S2

e: In adults, the spinal cord ends at L1–L2, and the vertebral level is approximately 2–3 segments higher than the spinal cord segment at lower levels. The L1 cord segment lies at the T10 vertebral level.
k: L1 spinal cord segment ≈ T10 vertebral level

e: In adults, the conus medullaris typically terminates at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). In neonates, it ends at L3.
k: Adult spinal cord ends at L1; neonatal spinal cord ends at L3

e: There is a discrepancy between vertebral and spinal cord levels in the thoracic region. The spinal cord segments are approximately 2 levels higher than their corresponding vertebrae in the lower thoracic region. A tumor at T4 would compress the T6 spinal cord segment.
k: Lower thoracic spinal cord segments are ~2 vertebral levels higher than the vertebrae

e: The sacral canal contains the filum terminale, cauda equina, cerebrospinal fluid, and the dural/arachnoid tube extending to S2. The ligamentum denticulatum anchors the spinal cord to the dura and does not extend into the sacral canal.
k: Ligamentum denticulatum is absent in the sacral canal

e: The spinal arachnoid mater extends to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2), where it fuses with the filum terminale.
k: Spinal arachnoid mater ends at S2

e: The leptomeninges consist of the pia mater and arachnoid mater. The dura mater is the outer meningeal layer and is not part of the leptomeninges.
k: Leptomeninges = pia + arachnoid mater

e: The spinal dura mater extends from the foramen magnum to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2). Below this, the filum terminale continues as the coccygeal ligament.
k: Spinal dura extends from foramen magnum to S2

e: The spinal cord is anchored to the dura mater by the denticulate ligaments (21 pairs), which are extensions of the pia mater located between the dorsal and ventral nerve roots.
k: Denticulate ligaments anchor the spinal cord to the dura

e: In adults, the conus medullaris typically ends at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). This is important clinically to avoid spinal cord injury during lumbar puncture, which is performed below this level.
k: Adult conus medullaris ends at lower border of L1

e: At birth, the spinal cord extends to the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). Due to differential growth of the vertebral column, the cord ascends to L1–L2 in adults.
k: Neonatal spinal cord ends at L3; adult at L1–L2

e: Lumbar puncture is performed below the level of the conus medullaris (which ends at L1–L2 in adults) to avoid cord injury. The needle is typically introduced at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace.
k: Lumbar puncture performed at L3–L4 or L4–L5 to avoid conus medullaris

e: At birth, the conus medullaris is located at the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). It ascends to L1–L2 by adulthood due to differential growth.
k: Birth conus medullaris at L3; ascends to L1–L2 in adults

e: In the thoracic region, the intervertebral disc is located above the corresponding numbered nerve root because the nerve exits below the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra. Therefore, a disc prolapse between T5 and T6 would compress the T6 nerve root as it exits.
k: Thoracic disc herniation at T5–T6 compresses the T6 nerve root

e: The spinal dura mater does NOT continue below L1 as the filum terminale. The filum terminale is a pial structure extending from the conus medullaris to the coccyx, pierced by the dura and arachnoid at S2. The dura itself ends at S2.
k: Filum terminale is pial, not dural; dura ends at S2

e: The first seven cervical nerves (C1–C7) emerge above their corresponding vertebrae. C8 emerges between C7 and T1. All other spinal nerves emerge below their corresponding vertebrae.
k: C1–C7 nerves emerge above their corresponding vertebrae

e: Due to the cephalad ascent of the spinal cord relative to the vertebral column during development, the upper 9 thoracic vertebrae contain the upper 10 thoracic spinal cord segments. There is approximately a 1–2 segment discrepancy.
k: Upper 9 thoracic vertebrae house the upper 10 thoracic cord segments

e: The dorsal root of the spinal nerve is purely sensory, containing afferent fibers from the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root is purely motor/efferent. The mixed spinal nerve trunk and its rami contain both sensory and motor fibers.
k: Dorsal root = purely sensory

e: The spinal cord segments above the level of the lower border of the fourth thoracic vertebra include 8 cervical + 4 thoracic = 12 segments.
k: 12 spinal cord segments lie above T4 vertebral level

e: The autonomic fibers arise from the lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) of the spinal cord gray matter, not the anterior horn. The posterior root carries sensory fibers and contains the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral root carries motor fibers.
k: Autonomic fibers arise from the lateral horn, not the anterior horn

e: Above the lower border of the ninth thoracic vertebra, the spinal cord contains 8 cervical + 9 thoracic = 17 segments. Due to differential growth, the cord segments are higher than their corresponding vertebrae.
k: 17 spinal cord segments lie above the T9 vertebral level

e: The intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn) contains the cell bodies of sympathetic preganglionic neurons and is located in the lateral horn of the spinal cord gray matter (T1–L2).
k: Intermediolateral cell column = lateral horn = sympathetic preganglionic neurons

e: The dorsal root ganglion cells are pseudounipolar (not multipolar). The central processes (axons) of dorsal root ganglion cells enter the spinal cord and may ascend or descend to form long tracts. The peripheral processes (dendrites) connect to receptors.
k: Dorsal root ganglion cells are pseudounipolar; central processes form ascending tracts

e: Nerve fibers within the gray matter are mostly unmyelinated or thinly myelinated, not heavily myelinated. Heavy myelination is characteristic of white matter tracts. The gray matter contains neuron cell bodies, dendrites, and glial cells.
k: Gray matter fibers are mostly unmyelinated; white matter fibers are myelinated

e: The intermediomedial nucleus is associated with the lateral horn and visceral afferent fibers, not the posterior horn. The posteromarginal nucleus is at the tip of the posterior horn. Nucleus proprius lies anterior to substantia gelatinosa.
k: Intermediomedial nucleus belongs to the lateral horn, not the posterior horn

e: The anteromedial nuclear group extends at all levels of the spinal cord and supplies the axial muscles. Alpha motor neurons supply extrafusal fibers; gamma motor neurons supply intrafusal fibers. The medial group supplies axial muscles, while the lateral group supplies limb muscles.
k: Anteromedial nucleus extends at all cord levels and supplies axial muscles

e: Lamina IV corresponds to the nucleus proprius (main sensory nucleus), not the reticular nucleus. The reticular nucleus corresponds to lamina V. Lamina II = substantia gelatinosa, lamina III = nucleus proprius, lamina VII includes Clarke's nucleus.
k: Lamina IV = nucleus proprius; lamina V = reticular nucleus
